messages.content:
You are an expert power-electronics designer synthesising the interface circuit of a
piezoelectric energy harvester. You work by experiment: you propose a circuit, it is simulated in
LTspice under several operating conditions, and you receive the measurements.

GOAL
A piezo transducer must power a sensor-node load RL from a storage capacitor at node "out".
Under EVERY operating condition below, starting from 0 V (cold start) and simulating 0.8 s:
  vout_min: vavg >= 1.8 V (settled mean output reaches the load's minimum supply)
  vout_max: vmax <= 3.6 V (output never exceeds the load's absolute maximum)
  ripple: vpp <= 0.05 V (peak-to-peak ripple in the final window)
  startup: tup <= 0.4 s (cold start: first time output reaches 1.8 V)
  settled: dv <= 0.02 V (mean output changes little between the last two windows)
Measurement windows: vavg and vpp over 0.7-0.8 s; vmax over the whole run; tup = first time
V(out) reaches 1.8 V (missing if never); dv = |mean(0.7-0.8 s) - mean(0.6-0.7 s)|.

PIEZO MODEL AND OPERATING CONDITIONS
The piezo is a sinusoidal current source Ip*sin(2*pi*f*t) in parallel with its capacitance Cp and a
20 MOhm leakage resistance, between nodes pzp and pzn (Cp = 25 nF nominal).
Its open-circuit voltage amplitude is Ip/(2*pi*f*Cp), about 3.2 V at nominal: low, so diode drops matter.
  S1: nominal; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S2: heavy load; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 150 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S3: strong excitation, light load; Ip = 100 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 2200 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S4: weak excitation; Ip = 30 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 1000 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S5: low frequency; Ip = 40 uA peak, f = 80 Hz, Cp = 25 nF, RL = 470 kOhm, temperature 27 C
  S6: Cp +20 %, hot; Ip = 50 uA peak, f = 100 Hz, Cp = 30 nF, RL = 330 kOhm, temperature 60 C

TEST BENCH (fixed, added automatically - do not include these)
- the piezo model between pzp and pzn; the load RL from out to 0;
- for every SYNC controller you use, a 0.5 uA supply current drawn from out (its power cost);
- a 1 GOhm resistor to 0 from pzp, pzn and every internal node (prevents floating nodes).

COMPONENTS YOU MAY USE (at most 16 components)
- R  resistor, value 1..1e+08 Ohm, nodes [a, b]
- C  capacitor, value 1e-10..4.7e-05 F, nodes [a, b]
- L  inductor, value 1e-05..0.01 H; it has series resistance 2 Ohm + 5 Ohm per mH
- D  diode, nodes [anode, cathode]: forward current flows from the first node to the second.
     Model one of DSCH, DSI, DZ33:
     DSCH = low-drop Schottky (~0.25 V at uA), DSI = silicon small-signal (~0.5 V at uA),
     DZ33 = 3.3 V zener (reverse breakdown 3.3 V, conducts ~1 uA at 3.3 V and much more above)
     Orientation matters:
       full bridge: ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"] (return diodes have
       their anode on ground);
       zener clamp on out: ["0", "out"] (cathode on out, so it is reverse-biased and breaks down at
       3.3 V). ["out", "0"] would be forward-biased and hold out near 0.7 V; it is rejected.
- S  switch, nodes [a, b], "ctrl": id of a SYNC; Ron = 2 Ohm, Roff = 1 GOhm (at most 4)
- SYNC ideal synchronous controller (no nodes, at most 2): closes its switches for "ton"
     seconds (1e-07..0.001) at the piezo voltage extrema, which occur at the zero
     crossings of the piezo current. "edges": "both" (every half period), "pos" (positive peak only)
     or "neg" (negative peak only). "phase" shifts the pulses by that fraction of the excitation
     period (-0.25..0.25). It tracks the excitation frequency automatically.
     For L-Cp inversion, ton is about pi*sqrt(L*Cp).
Nodes: "0" is ground; pzp, pzn are the piezo terminals; out is the load/storage node; name any other
nodes yourself (lower-case, e.g. n1, mid). Every node needs at least two connections, and out must
connect to the piezo through your circuit.

REFERENCE DESIGN: FBR (full-bridge rectifier, 4 x DSCH, 2.2 uF on out). Its results:
cond   vavg V  vmax V  vpp mV   tup s  Pload uW  vout_min vout_max ripple   startup  settled 
S1       2.24    2.25    26.2   0.269      15.2  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S2       1.76    1.77    20.3       -      20.7  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     ok      
S3       5.68    5.72    84.4  0.0779      14.7  ok       FAIL     FAIL     ok       FAIL    
S4       1.51    1.52    20.8       -      2.27  FAIL     ok       ok       FAIL     FAIL    
S5       2.26    2.28    43.5   0.318      10.9  ok       ok       ok       ok       FAIL    
S6       1.93    1.94    18.8   0.379      11.3  ok       ok       ok       ok       ok      

HOW TO WORK
- Component values are optimised automatically (an evolution strategy, up to 48 full
  evaluations per structure, running while you think), so spend your reasoning on circuit
  CONNECTIVITY (topology): which structure can meet every condition. A structure that was already
  explored is not simulated again, whatever its values.
- Each proposal is first SCREENED: with out fixed at 1.8 V, the net power it delivers is
  measured on S2, S4, S6 for its proposed values and a few automatic value presets.
  If the best preset delivers less than 50 % of the load's need (V^2/RL) on any of them,
  the design is reported back with those powers and is not tuned or simulated further.
- Each round, propose up to 3 designs with DIFFERENT connectivity (different structures, not value variants).
- Classify each design with "move": new_topology or modify_topology, and explain the expected effect
  in "rationale". Set "done": true only when you believe no further structural change can improve on
  the best design so far.
- Reply with ONE JSON object only, in this form:
{
 "proposals": [
  {
   "move": "new_topology",
   "name": "short label for this design",
   "rationale": "what you changed and why it should fix the failing checks",
   "done": false,
   "components": [
    {
     "id": "D1",
     "type": "D",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "out"
     ],
     "model": "DSCH"
    },
    {
     "id": "C1",
     "type": "C",
     "nodes": [
      "out",
      "0"
     ],
     "value": 2.2e-06
    },
    {
     "id": "L1",
     "type": "L",
     "nodes": [
      "pzp",
      "n1"
     ],
     "value": 0.0047
    },
    {
     "id": "S1",
     "type": "S",
     "nodes": [
      "n1",
      "pzn"
     ],
     "ctrl": "G1"
    },
    {
     "id": "G1",
     "type": "SYNC",
     "ton": 3.4e-05,
     "phase": 0.0,
     "edges": "both"
    }
   ]
  }
 ]
}

Round 1 of 12.

This is your first round: choose the structures you think most likely to meet every condition.

Reply with one JSON object only.

*   Goal: Power a sensor load $R_L$ from a piezo harvester.
    *   Constraints:
        *   $V_{out\_min} \ge 1.8\text{V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $V_{out\_max} \le 3.6\text{V}$ (S1-S6)
        *   $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$ (ripple)
        *   $t_{up} \le 0.4\text{s}$ (startup)
        *   $dv \le 0.02\text{V}$ (settled)
    *   Piezo Model: Current source $I_p \sin(2\pi f t)$ in parallel with $C_p$ (25nF) and $R_{leak} = 20\text{M}\Omega$.
    *   Voltage amplitude is low (~3.2V), so diode drops are significant.
    *   The reference design (FBR: Full Bridge Rectifier) failed on $V_{out\_min}$ for S2, S4; $V_{out\_max}$ and $V_{pp}$ for S3; and settlement for S1, S5.

    *   S1 (Nominal): $I_p = 50\mu\text{A}, f=100\text{Hz}, C_p=25\text{nF}, R_L=330\text{k}\Omega$.
    *   S2 (Heavy Load): $I_p = 50\mu\text{A}, f=100\text{Hz}, C_p=25\text{nF}, R_L=150\text{k}\Omega$. (Low voltage risk)
    *   S3 (Strong/Light): $I_p = 100\mu\text{A}, f=100\text{Hz}, C_p=25\text{nF}, R_L=2.2\text{M}\Omega$. (Overvoltage risk)
    *   S4 (Weak): $I_p = 30\mu\text{A}, f=100\text{Hz}, C_p=25\text{nF}, R_L=1\text{M}\Omega$. (Low voltage risk)
    *   S5 (Low freq): $I_p = 40\mu\text{A}, f=80\text{Hz}, C_p=25\text{nF}, R_L=470\text{k}\Omega$.
    *   S6 (Hot/Cap+): $I_p = 50\mu\text{A}, f=100\text{Hz}, C_p=30\text{nF}, R_L=330\text{k}\Omega$.

    *   The open-circuit voltage $V_{oc} \approx \frac{I_p}{2\pi f C_p}$. For S1, $V_{oc} \approx 3.18\text{V}$.
    *   A full bridge rectifier has two diode drops ($\approx 0.5\text{V}$ combined for DSCH). This reduces available voltage and efficiency.
    *   The load range is wide (150k to 2.2M), and excitation varies (30uA to 100uA).
    *   We need a way to:
        1.  Increase efficiency to meet $V_{out\_min}$ (avoid 2 diode drops).
        2.  Limit $V_{out}$ to 3.6V for S3.
        3.  Ensure low ripple (large $C_{out}$ or active regulation).

    *   **Topology 1: Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction (SECE) or SSHI (Synchronized Switch Harvesting on Inductor).**
        SSHI can significantly increase the extracted power by flipping the voltage across $C_p$ at the peaks.
        A basic SSHI structure involves a switch and an inductor.
        Given the components, a "Partial SSHI" or "Parallel-SSHI" might work.
        *Connectivity:* Piezo $\rightarrow$ Rectifier $\rightarrow$ Storage. Inductor/Switch used to flip $C_p$.
        Wait, the SYNC controller closes the switch at extrema.
        If we put a switch and inductor in parallel with the piezo (pzp, pzn), we can flip the charge.
        Actually, a common simple SSHI is:
        Piezo (pzp, pzn) $\rightarrow$ Full bridge $\rightarrow$ Storage.
        An inductor $L$ and switch $S$ in parallel with the piezo to flip $V_{Cp}$.
        Wait, the provided components allow a SYNC controller.
        Let's try a "Synchronous Rectifier" or an SSHI-like charge pump.

    *   **Topology 2: Zener-clamped FBR.**
        The FBR failed $V_{out\_max}$ for S3. A Zener diode (DZ33) on the output can clamp $V_{out}$ to 3.3V.
        But FBR failed $V_{out\_min}$ for S2 and S4. We need more power.

    *   **Topology 3: Synchronous Switch Harvesting (Simplified SSHI).**
        Connect an inductor $L$ and switch $S$ across the piezo. This flips the voltage $V_{Cp}$ at the peaks, effectively increasing the voltage seen by the rectifier.
        *Circuit:*
        1. Full Bridge (DSCH) from pzp, pzn to out, 0.
        2. L and S in parallel with pzp, pzn.
        3. SYNC controller for S.
        4. Storage C on out.
        5. Zener clamp (DZ33) on out to prevent S3 from exceeding 3.6V.

    *   **Topology 4: Active Rectification / Charge Pump.**
        If we use the SYNC switch as a transfer switch.
        Example: Piezo $\rightarrow$ Switch $\rightarrow$ Capacitor.
        But the SYNC is ideal (Ron=2 Ohm).
        A simple "half-bridge" synchronous rectifier might be too complex.

    Let's refine the SSHI-like approach.
    The goal is to avoid the efficiency loss of 2 diodes if possible, or at least increase the voltage.
    Standard SSHI:
    - Piezo (pzp, pzn)
    - Rectifier: pzp $\rightarrow$ D1 $\rightarrow$ out, pzn $\rightarrow$ D2 $\rightarrow$ out, 0 $\rightarrow$ D3 $\rightarrow$ pzp, 0 $\rightarrow$ D4 $\rightarrow$ pzn. (Full bridge)
    - Flipping circuit: pzp $\rightarrow$ L1 $\rightarrow$ S1 $\rightarrow$ pzn.
    - S1 is controlled by SYNC (edges: "both", phase: 0).

    Wait, the Reference Design was a basic FBR.
    FBR results:
    S2 (150k): 1.76V (Fail, need 1.8V)
    S4 (1M): 1.51V (Fail, need 1.8V)
    S3 (2.2M): 5.68V (Fail, need 3.6V)

    To fix S2/S4, we need more power. SSHI increases power.
    To fix S3, we need a clamp. DZ33 is perfect.

    *Let's check if there's a simpler way to avoid the double diode drop.*
    A half-bridge rectifier (using the SYNC switch) could work.
    Example:
    pzp $\rightarrow$ S1 $\rightarrow$ out
    pzn $\rightarrow$ S2 $\rightarrow$ out
    (But we only have 2 SYNCs and 4 switches total).
    Using 2 SYNCs:
    SYNC1: edges="pos", phase=0, S1 [pzp, out]
    SYNC2: edges="neg", phase=0, S2 [pzn, out]
    This is basically a synchronous rectifier. It would eliminate the diode drops.
    However, if $V_{out}$ is already 3V and $V_{pzp}$ is 2V, the switch will dump charge from the capacitor back into the piezo. We need diodes to prevent this.
    So:
    pzp $\rightarrow$ D1 $\rightarrow$ S1 $\rightarrow$ out
    pzn $\rightarrow$ D2 $\rightarrow$ S2 $\rightarrow$ out
    (Still has diode drops).

    Let's go back to SSHI. It's a proven technique for low-voltage piezos.
    Structure:
    - Full Bridge (D1-D4)
    - Parallel L-S (L1, S1) for flipping
    - Output Cap (Cout)
    - Zener Clamp (D_zener)

    Let's reconsider the "S" components.
    S is a switch.
    If I use a SYNC and a switch for SSHI, it's:
    - L1: [pzp, n1]
    - S1: [n1, pzn], ctrl: G1
    - G1: SYNC, edges: "both", phase: 0.
    This flips the voltage.

    Wait, the "Reference Design" FBR used a 2.2uF cap.
    Let's try to improve it.

    **Proposal 1: SSHI + Clamp**
    - Full Bridge (D1-D4)
    - L1, S1 in parallel with piezo
    - C1 (storage)
    - D5 (Zener DZ33) for clamping
    - G1 (SYNC) for flipping

    **Proposal 2: Synchronous Rectifier (simplified)**
    - S1 [pzp, out], ctrl: G1 (edges: pos)
    - S2 [pzn, out], ctrl: G2 (edges: neg)
    - D1 [out, pzp], D2 [out, pzn] (to prevent reverse flow?) No, that's not right.
    - Actually, the simplest "power boost" is the SSHI.

    **Proposal 3: Half-bridge with Inductor (Boost-like)**
    Since the voltage is low, maybe a boost converter? But we only have SYNC.
    SYNC is designed for "piezo voltage extrema". This is exactly what's needed for SSHI or SECE.

    Let's double-check the "S" and "SYNC" limits.
    - At most 4 switches (S).
    - At most 2 SYNC controllers (G).
    - Max 16 components.

    *SSHI Circuit Construction:*
    - D1: [pzp, out], model: DSCH
    - D2: [pzn, out], model: DSCH
    - D3: [0, pzp], model: DSCH
    - D4: [0, pzn], model: DSCH
    - L1: [pzp, n1], value: 10mH (starting)
    - S1: [n1, pzn], ctrl: G1
    - G1: SYNC, ton: 50us, edges: "both", phase: 0
    - C1: [out, 0], value: 10uF
    - D5: [0, out], model: DZ33 (Zener clamp)

    Wait, the "full bridge" in the reference was:
    ["pzp", "out"], ["pzn", "out"], ["0", "pzp"], ["0", "pzn"]
    Wait, this is not a standard bridge.
    Standard bridge:
    Anode pzp, Cathode out (D1)
    Anode pzn, Cathode out (D2)
    Anode 0, Cathode pzp (D3)
    Anode 0, Cathode pzn (D4)
    Let's trace:
    When pzp is high, pzn is low:
    pzp $\rightarrow$ D1 $\rightarrow$ out.
    0 $\rightarrow$ D4 $\rightarrow$ pzn. (Current path: 0 $\rightarrow$ D4 $\rightarrow$ pzn $\rightarrow$ piezo $\rightarrow$ pzp $\rightarrow$ D1 $\rightarrow$ out).
    When pzn is high, pzp is low:
    pzn $\rightarrow$ D2 $\rightarrow$ out.
    0 $\rightarrow$ D3 $\rightarrow$ pzp. (Current path: 0 $\rightarrow$ D3 $\rightarrow$ pzp $\rightarrow$ piezo $\rightarrow$ pzn $\rightarrow$ D2 $\rightarrow$ out).
    Yes, that's a full bridge.

    *Wait, look at the reference design results again.*
    S3: vavg=5.68V, vmax=5.72V. (Too high)
    S4: vavg=1.51V. (Too low)
    S2: vavg=1.76V. (Too low)
    So SSHI should help S2/S4, and DZ33 should fix S3.

    Is there any other topology?
    Maybe a "charge pump" using the switches?
    Pzp $\rightarrow$ S1 $\rightarrow$ C_mid $\rightarrow$ S2 $\rightarrow$ out.
    But we have a sinusoidal current source.

    Let's try a second topology just in case: **A Voltage Doubler**.
    A piezo is basically a capacitor. A voltage doubler (Greinacher) can increase the output voltage.
    - D1: [pzp, n1]
    - C1: [n1, 0]
    - D2: [n1, out]
    - C2: [out, 0]
    But this only works for one half-cycle.
    For both half-cycles:
    - D1: [pzp, n1]
    - D2: [pzn, n1]
    - C1: [n1, 0]
    - D3: [n1, out]
    - C2: [out, 0]
    This is basically a center-tapped rectifier. But pzp/pzn are the only terminals.
    Wait, if we use the SYNC switches:
    - S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1 (pos)
    - S2: [pzn, n1], ctrl: G1 (neg)
    - C1: [n1, 0]
    - S3: [n1, out], ctrl: G2 ... (this is getting complex).

    Let's stick to SSHI and a simple FBR with Zener.
    Actually, let's try:
    1. SSHI + Zener (The "Powerhouse")
    2. FBR + Zener (The "Safe" one - maybe just the cap value was wrong)
    3. SSHI without Zener (to see if it's better) - No, S3 will fail.

    One more thing: The SYNC "ton" for L-Cp inversion.
    $t_{on} \approx \pi \sqrt{L C_p}$.
    $C_p = 25\text{nF}$, $L = 10\text{mH} \implies t_{on} \approx 3.14 \times \sqrt{10^{-2} \times 25 \cdot 10^{-9}} = 3.14 \times \sqrt{2.5 \cdot 10^{-10}} \approx 3.14 \times 1.58 \cdot 10^{-5} \approx 50\mu\text{s}$.

    Let's refine the components for the SSHI proposal.
    L1 = 10mH, C1 = 10uF, ton = 50us.

    Wait, the Reference Design had $C_{out} = 2.2\mu\text{F}$.
    Ripple requirement: $V_{pp} \le 0.05\text{V}$.
    $V_{pp} \approx \frac{I_{load}}{f C_{out}}$.
    For S2: $R_L = 150\text{k}\Omega, V_{out} = 1.8\text{V} \implies I_{load} = 12\mu\text{A}$.
    $f = 100\text{Hz}$ (but rectification makes it 200Hz).
    $V_{pp} \approx \frac{12\mu\text{A}}{200 \times 2.2\mu\text{F}} \approx \frac{12}{440} \approx 0.027\text{V}$.
    So $2.2\mu\text{F}$ is actually enough for ripple. The main problem is $V_{avg}$.

    *Self-Correction on SSHI:*
    In a real SSHI, the switch $S$ is in parallel with the piezo, and the rectifier is *after* the flipping.
    The current flow is:
    1. Piezo charges $C_p$.
    2. At peak, $S$ closes, $L$ and $C_p$ resonate, $V_{Cp}$ flips.
    3. The rectifier then takes the "extra" voltage.
    Actually, the flip increases the voltage swing, so the rectifier sees a higher peak voltage.

    Let's try these three:
    1.  **SSHI-Zener**: Full bridge + L/S flip + Zener clamp.
    2.  **FBR-Zener**: Full bridge + Zener clamp (to see if FBR can pass S3, and maybe $C_{out}$ optimization fixes the rest).
    3.  **SSHI-LDO**: (Wait, no LDO available). Let's try SSHI with a different $L$ or different $S$ configuration.
        Actually, maybe a "half-bridge" synchronous rectifier?
        No, the "Reference Design" already showed FBR fails on $V_{out\_min}$.
        Let's try **SSHI with a different switch timing**.

    Wait, is there any other way to get more voltage?
    What if I use the SYNC switch as a way to bypass diodes?
    S1 [pzp, out], ctrl: G1 (pos peak)
    S2 [pzn, out], ctrl: G2 (neg peak)
    But without diodes, when $V_{out} > V_{pzp}$, the capacitor will discharge back into the piezo.
    Unless the SYNC switch is *only* closed for a very short time $t_{on}$.
    This is exactly what a "Synchronous Rectifier" does.
    But for it to work, the switch must be closed when $V_{pzp} > V_{out}$.
    The SYNC controller closes at "piezo voltage extrema".
    At the positive peak, $V_{pzp}$ is at its maximum. If $V_{pzp\_max} > V_{out}$, closing S1 for a short time $t_{on}$ will transfer charge.
    This is called "Synchronous Electric Charge Extraction" (SECE).
    SECE Topology:
    - S1 [pzp, out], ctrl: G1 (edges: pos)
    - S2 [pzn, out], ctrl: G2 (edges: neg)
    - C1 [out, 0]
    - (Need a way to prevent reverse flow? The $t_{on}$ is very short, so it might be okay, but usually, you'd want a diode).
    - Actually, SECE usually uses a diode to prevent backflow: pzp $\rightarrow$ D1 $\rightarrow$ S1 $\rightarrow$ out.
    But the $t_{on}$ is so small (1e-7 to 1ms) that the charge transferred is $Q = \int I dt$.
    If $V_{pzp} > V_{out}$, current flows to the capacitor.
    If $V_{pzp} < V_{out}$, current flows from the capacitor.
    Since the SYNC triggers at the peak, $V_{pzp}$ is likely $> V_{out}$ for a small window.

    Let's try:
    1. SSHI-Zener (Best bet for power and clamping)
    2. SECE-Zener (Another way to increase power)
    3. FBR-Zener (Baseline with clamp)

    *Refining SECE-Zener:*
    - S1 [pzp, out], ctrl: G1 (pos, ton=100us)
    - S2 [pzn, out], ctrl: G2 (neg, ton=100us)
    - D1 [out, pzp], D2 [out, pzn] (No, that's not right).
    Wait, in SECE, you just need a switch and a diode:
    pzp $\rightarrow$ D1 $\rightarrow$ S1 $\rightarrow$ out
    pzn $\rightarrow$ D2 $\rightarrow$ S2 $\rightarrow$ out
    And a Zener clamp on out.

    Let's compare SSHI and SECE.
    SSHI flips $V_{Cp}$, effectively increasing the voltage available for the rectifier.
    SECE extracts charge at the peak.
    SSHI is generally more efficient for piezo.

    *Final check on components for SSHI-Zener:*
    - D1: [pzp, out], model: DSCH
    - D2: [pzn, out], model: DSCH
    - D3: [0, pzp], model: DSCH
    - D4: [0, pzn], model: DSCH
    - L1: [pzp, n1], value: 10mH
    - S1: [n1, pzn], ctrl: G1
    - G1: SYNC, ton: 50us, edges: "both", phase: 0
    - C1: [out, 0], value: 2.2uF
    - D5: [0, out], model: DZ33

    *Final check on components for SECE-Zener:*
    - S1: [pzp, n1], ctrl: G1 (pos)
    - S2: [pzn, n2], ctrl: G2 (neg)
    - D1: [n1, out], model: DSCH
    - D2: [n2, out], model: DSCH
    - C1: [out, 0], value: 2.2uF
    - D3: [0, out], model: DZ33
    - G1: SYNC, ton: 100us, edges: "pos"
    - G2: SYNC, ton: 100us, edges: "neg"

    *Final check on components for FBR-Zener:*
    - D1: [pzp, out], model: DSCH
    - D2: [pzn, out], model: DSCH
    - D3: [0, pzp], model: DSCH
    - D4: [0, pzn], model: DSCH
    - C1: [out, 0], value: 2.2uF
    - D5: [0, out], model: DZ33

    One detail: the SYNC controllers "track the excitation frequency automatically".
    The "phase" shifts the pulses. For SSHI, the flip should happen at the voltage peak.
    The SYNC controller triggers at "piezo voltage extrema", which are the "zero crossings of the piezo current".
    So phase 0.0 should be correct.

    Let's use these three.

    *Wait, one more thing:*
    The "Reference Design" FBR failed the "settled" check (dv <= 0.02 V) for S1 and S5.
    This means the output was still drifting.
    A larger $C_{out}$ might slow down the drift, but the problem is likely that the energy harvested didn't match the load exactly.
    The "settled" check is $dv = |mean(0.7-0.8) - mean(0.6-0.7)|$.
